Keen

/keen/ — rhymes with seen · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Keen describes a feeling, such as an interest or desire, that is unusually eager and intense.

Maya has a keen interest in astronomy and stays up late to watch meteor showers.

Worked Example

After years of waiting, the young dancer finally auditioned for the ballet company, her keen desire to join driving every leap and pirouette.

Keen captures both intense eagerness and deep investment — the definition specifies this combination. Plain words like 'eager' miss the depth and intensity; 'strong desire' lacks the sense of sharp focus. Keen is more precise.

How Keen Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

eager

eager: excited and impatient to get started

avid

avid: enthusiastically devoted to an interest

ardent

ardent: burning with passionate, devoted feeling, as for a cause or a love; keen is cooler - a sharp, eager interest without the emotional blaze

Antonyms

indifferent

indifferent: having no interest or concern at all

apathetic

apathetic: feeling no enthusiasm, energy, or concern

How Strong Is It? — disinterested → interested → eager → keen

disinterested vs. keen

disinterested vs. keen: Disinterested sits at the bottom, far below keen: a disinterested person feels no pull toward the subject at all, while a keen one is intensely eager about it.

interested vs. keen

interested vs. keen: Interested is much weaker than keen: an interested person pays attention when the topic comes up, while a keen person actively seeks it out with intense eagerness.

eager vs. keen

eager vs. keen: Eager is strong, but keen is a notch stronger — an eager person looks forward to something, while a keen person's interest has an unusually sharp, intense edge.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cene

Root — cene: bold, brave; sharp, skilled (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Keen comes straight from Old English cene, 'bold and sharp,' with no added prefixes or suffixes. A keen blade has a sharp edge — and a keen interest carries that same sharp, intense edge of eagerness.

Use the root in a new word: keenness

Use the root in a new word: keenness: Her keenness for chess showed in the way she studied openings at lunch — keenness is simply the noun built directly on keen, meaning sharp eagerness.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Keen captures intense, eager interest — use it when the feeling is strong and sustained. For mild or passing interest, 'interested' or 'eager' works better.
